specPoints.text: know the general formula for alkanes
explain why alkanes are classified as saturated hydrocarbons
understand how to draw the structural and displayed formulae for alkanes with up to five carbon atoms in the molecule, and to name the unbranched-chain isomers

primer.text: From Cracking you already know that alkanes are the single-bonded products the column delivers in bulk. This note formalises the family: the general formula that generates every member, why the family is called saturated, and the names and drawings of the first five alkanes.

lessons.title: The saturated family and its formula
lessons.opening: Alkanes are the quiet workhorses of organic chemistry, unreactive but everywhere. This lesson fixes the two labels the exam rewards: their general formula and the word saturated.
keyPoints: Alkanes are a group of saturated hydrocarbons, meaning they have single carbon-carbon bonds only.
No double bonds exist anywhere in an alkane molecule, which is what saturated means here.
The general formula of the alkanes is CnH2n+2, with n a whole number.
Alkanes are generally unreactive but burn, can be cracked, and react with halogens in light.
Methane, the first alkane, is the major component of natural gas.

low.restatement: Alkanes hold hands with single bonds only: every carbon-to-carbon link is single, so they are called saturated. Their formula recipe is CnH2n+2. Add two hydrogens for every carbon and the formula writes itself.
low.analogy: A saturated alkane is a shelf filled to capacity with single-strength links; no spare grip remains for another bond, which is why the family is so calm.
low.examPointer: When asked why alkanes are saturated, say single carbon-carbon bonds only and no double bonds.

medium.restatement: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons because their carbon atoms are joined by single bonds alone, with no double bond anywhere to open. The family follows the general formula CnH2n+2, and its members are largely unreactive apart from burning, being cracked and reacting with halogens under light.
medium.analogy: Picture a chain of people holding one hand each with their neighbours and one spare hand raised to hydrogen: every grip is taken, so newcomers must find chemistry elsewhere.
medium.examPointer: Substitute n values into CnH2n+2 to check any given alkane formula, and quote the single-bond rule for the saturated label.

check.stem: What does saturated mean for an alkane?

options.text: It has only single carbon-carbon bonds and no double bonds
options.explanation: Single bonds only is the exact sense in which alkanes are called saturated.

options.text: It is dissolved in water to full concentration
options.explanation: Saturation here describes bonding, not solutions.

options.text: It contains the maximum possible oxygen
options.explanation: Alkanes contain no oxygen at all.

options.text: It cannot undergo any reaction whatsoever
options.explanation: Alkanes burn, crack and react with halogens; they are just generally unreactive.

check.stem: An alkane has n = 3. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: C3H8
options.explanation: Substituting gives H = 2(3) + 2 = 8, so propane is C3H8.

options.text: C3H6
options.explanation: That is CnH2n, the alkene recipe, not the alkane one.

options.text: C3H10
options.explanation: Two extra hydrogens break both the formula and the bonding rules.

options.text: C2H8
options.explanation: The carbon count must match n, which is three here.

check.stem: Why are alkanes classified as hydrocarbons?

options.text: Because they contain only hydrogen and carbon atoms
options.explanation: The CnH2n+2 recipe uses exactly those two elements and no others.

options.text: Because they were first found in living things
options.explanation: Origin plays no part in the hydrocarbon definition.

options.text: Because they always contain a C=C bond
options.explanation: A C=C bond would make them alkenes and unsaturated.

options.text: Because they burn to give carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Burning behaviour is a consequence, not the classification test.

options.text: Combustion, cracking, and reaction with halogens in light
options.explanation: The note lists exactly these three as the chemistry of this generally unreactive family.

options.text: They react readily with most reagents at room temperature
options.explanation: Alkanes are described as generally unreactive; their chemistry is a short list.

options.text: None at all, because they are fully saturated
options.explanation: Saturation limits but does not abolish reactivity.

options.text: Only addition reactions across their double bonds
options.explanation: Alkanes have no double bonds to add across; that is alkene chemistry.

check.stem: Why is methane described as the major component of natural gas?

options.text: Because natural gas consists mainly of CH4 molecules
options.explanation: The note identifies methane as the principal ingredient of natural gas.

options.text: Because natural gas is pure liquid methane
options.explanation: Natural gas is gaseous and mainly, not purely, methane.

options.text: Because methane is the largest alkane molecule
options.explanation: Methane is the smallest alkane; its role comes from abundance.

options.text: Because natural gas contains no other elements
options.explanation: The statement is about which molecule dominates, not element purity.

lessons.title: Naming and drawing the first five
lessons.opening: The first five alkanes are the exam currency of this family. This lesson lines up methane through pentane with their molecular formulae and shows how the displayed drawings follow the formula.
keyPoints: The first five alkanes are methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10 and pentane C5H12.
Each displayed formula draws every bond: four single bonds round each carbon atom.
Methane has one carbon, so its displayed formula shows that carbon bonded to four hydrogens.
Ethane, propane, butane and pentane extend the carbon chain one carbon at a time.
Exams ask you to name, draw and give the formula for the first five alkanes.

low.restatement: Learn the run of five: methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, with hydrogens 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Each drawing simply shows single bonds joining the carbons and hydrogens.
low.analogy: It is a ladder where each rung adds one carbon block and two hydrogen rungs; climb from CH4 to C5H12 without skipping.
low.examPointer: Practise drawing each displayed formula with every bond shown; half-drawn structures lose the mark.

medium.restatement: The homologous run runs methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10 and pentane C5H12, each obeying CnH2n+2. Drawing a displayed formula means every single bond appears, so each carbon shows four bonds whether to neighbouring carbons or to hydrogens.
medium.analogy: Think of carbon as a four-way junction: in every alkane drawing, all four arms must be filled, and the chain grows by inserting extra junctions one at a time.
medium.examPointer: Check every carbon in your drawing carries four bonds before moving on; a carbon with three or five is the classic lost mark.

check.stem: Which molecular formula belongs to pentane?

options.text: C5H12
options.explanation: With n = 5 the alkane recipe gives H = 2(5) + 2 = 12.

options.text: C5H10
options.explanation: That is the alkene count for five carbons; the alkane needs two more hydrogens.

options.text: C4H10
options.explanation: Four carbons is butane, one rung below pentane.

options.text: C5H8
options.explanation: That formula fits no unbranched alkane or alkene of five carbons.

check.stem: How many hydrogen atoms appear in the displayed formula of ethane?

options.explanation: Ethane is C2H6: two carbons joined to each other, each carrying three hydrogens.
Four hydrogens would leave two carbon bonds unfilled.
Eight hydrogens is propane count territory, not ethane.
Two hydrogens would suit no saturated two-carbon skeleton.

check.stem: Which name follows propane in the alkane series?

options.text: Butane
options.explanation: The stems run meth, eth, prop, but, pent; so butane follows propane.

options.text: Pentane
options.explanation: Pentane comes after butane, two rungs above propane.

options.text: Ethane
options.explanation: Ethane is below propane in the series.

options.text: Propene
options.explanation: That is the three-carbon alkene, a different family.

check.stem: In the displayed formula of propane, what bonds does the middle carbon carry?

options.text: Two bonds to carbon neighbours and two to hydrogen atoms
options.explanation: Four bonds fill the middle carbon: one to each chain neighbour plus two hydrogens.

options.text: Four bonds to hydrogen atoms
options.explanation: That describes the end carbons of methane or an isolated carbon, not a middle carbon.

options.text: A double bond to one neighbour
options.explanation: Alkanes carry single bonds only; a double bond would break the family rule.

options.text: Three bonds, with one spare
options.explanation: Carbon always shows four bonds in these displayed structures.

check.stem: What must a full displayed formula of butane show that a molecular formula does not?

options.text: Every individual bond between the atoms
options.explanation: C4H10 counts atoms; the displayed formula draws all thirteen bonds in place.

options.text: The boiling point of the compound
options.explanation: Physical data belongs to tables, not drawings.

options.text: The colour of the liquid
options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant to a structural drawing.

options.text: The simplest ratio of atoms
options.explanation: Ratios are the empirical formula job; displayed means every bond drawn.

glossary.definition: A saturated hydrocarbon of the family with general formula CnH2n+2 and single bonds only.
Describing a hydrocarbon whose carbon atoms are joined by single bonds only, with no double bonds.
A formula pattern using n that generates every member of a homologous series, such as CnH2n+2.
A drawing showing every atom and every bond in the molecule explicitly.
The fossil fuel consisting mainly of methane molecules.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the general formula of the alkanes. b) Use it to work out the molecular formulae of propane (n = 3) and pentane (n = 5). c) Explain why alkanes are classified as saturated hydrocarbons.
steps: a) The general formula of the alkanes is CnH2n+2, where n is a whole number.
b) For propane, 2 x 3 + 2 = 8, so the formula is C3H8; for pentane, 2 x 5 + 2 = 12, so the formula is C5H12.
c) Saturated means the carbon atoms are joined by single bonds only, with no double bonds anywhere in the molecule.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) CnH2n+2. b) Propane C3H8; pentane C5H12. c) Single carbon-carbon bonds only — no double bonds.
